name: FAIR Data
title: FAIR Data
answer: FAIR Data is a set of guiding principles for research data management, first published in 2016, that asks data to be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable. It applies to datasets, metadata, code and the repositories that hold them, across every discipline that produces research outputs. The principles are about how data is described and shared, not about making all data open, since access terms can still be restricted. For an AI researcher, FAIR matters because training and evaluation depend on data that can be located, understood and lawfully combined with other sources.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: FAIR Data is a set of guiding principles for research data management, first published in 2016, that asks data to be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable. It applies to datasets, metadata, code and the repositories that hold them, across every discipline that produces research outputs. The principles are about how data is described and shared, not about making all data open, since access terms can still be restricted. For an AI researcher, FAIR matters because training and evaluation depend on data that can be located, understood and lawfully combined with other sources.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: FAIR data runs on repositories, persistent identifiers, metadata standards and machine readable licences. DOIs anchor a dataset to a citable record, while schema such as DataCite metadata and vocabularies like schema.org describe what the data is and how it may be used. Domain repositories such as Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad and institutional archives provide storage and versioning, and catalogues index those records so they can be discovered. The site's own library of 804 scientific models and 850 AI tools shows the same pattern, where a record points to an original source rather than a summary.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by planning data management before collection, choosing a repository, assigning identifiers and writing metadata that both people and machines can read. Researchers document variables, units, provenance and licence terms, then deposit the data with a version history and a citation. Interoperability is achieved by using common formats and controlled vocabularies rather than bespoke spreadsheets. Assessment is often done with FAIR maturity checklists or automated metadata validators, which score a record on how completely it can be found and reused.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk sit with the data owner, the repository and the funder, and FAIR does not override privacy, consent or intellectual property law. Personal data must be de-identified or access controlled, and sensitive or dual use data may be described openly while remaining restricted. Provenance records who created the data, how it was processed and under what licence, which supports attribution and reproducibility. The site's practice of linking to the original paper rather than a search tool reflects the same principle, that a claim should trace back to its source.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward machine actionable metadata, so that agents can discover and combine datasets without human mediation. Funders and journals increasingly require a data availability statement and a FAIR compliant deposit, and repository certification schemes are becoming more common. Work continues on persistent identifiers for people, instruments and samples, and on metrics that reward data sharing in research assessment. The open question is how to keep FAIR practical for small teams while meeting growing expectations for documentation and reuse.
